raw_case_text:
The present case describes a 47-year-old female patient with a history of chronic kidney disease requiring during an acute episode, referred to the Dermatology department with nodular lesions and abscesses, presenting purulent secretion drainage, which appeared primarily at the site of a Shilley catheter implantation in the right subclavian vein four months before. The lesions spread to the abdomen, anterior and posterior thorax, and were painful to palpation. The patient denied systemic symptoms such as fever, unintentional weight loss, and night sweats. Empirical treatment with antimicrobials (ciprofloxacin and cephalexin) was instituted, without improvement of the condition.
On physical examination, several nodules and subcutaneous tumors measuring up to six centimeters in their largest axis were observed, covered by slightly desquamative erythematous-violaceous skin with an ulcerated center, some of which showed spontaneous drainage of purulent secretion (Fig. 1).
Fine-needle aspiration biopsy guided by dermatological ultrasound was performed on a lesion in the posterior thorax (the largest lesion). The collected material was sent to the microbiology laboratory for culture of aerobic, anaerobic and micro bacteria, which did not show growth of bacterial colonies, and to the parasitology laboratory, where direct examination showed structures compatible with cysts and trophozoites of Entamoeba histolytica (Fig. 2). A skin biopsy was also performed, and histopathology showed an histiocytic reaction surrounding abscesses in the superficial and deep dermis, with trophozoites of Entamoeba histolytica identified on high power microscopy (Fig. 3).
Additional tests were performed to investigate involvement in other organs by the parasites. The parasitological stool examination was negative in three samples for helminths and protozoa, and computed tomography scans of the abdomen and pelvis did not show the presence of a liver or intestinal abscess.
Laboratory tests performed before and after treatment did not show any changes in liver enzymes, either canalicular or transaminases. The patient had normocytic and normochromic anemia related to her underlying disease.
Oral treatment with metronidazole 250 mg every eight hours for 20 days combined with ivermectin 12 mg, in a single dose, was performed. The patient was reevaluated 30 days after the end of metronidazole therapy, showing significant improvement in the lesions, with regression of the nodules and subcutaneous tumors, absence of erythema, and only residual hyperchromia (Fig. 4).
Amebiasis is a public health problem worldwide, particularly in developing countries. The first reports were probably made by Hippocrates, who discussed dysentery associated with inflammation of the liver. However, cutaneous involvement is extremely rare. Review studies that assess decades of care and scientific publications show modest numbers of at most 26 cases in children and adults.
Although the cutaneous lesions can occur anywhere in the body, anogenital ulcers are the main manifestation, and the location has been reported in both children and adults. The trophozoites are continually shed and the surrounding skin undergoes repeated trauma, which is the main mechanism of infection: the amoebae escape from the intestine to the adjacent skin. Transmission can also occur through contact with contaminated fomites, as well as through sexual intercourse. Hematogenous dissemination occurs when the trophozoites carried by the bloodstream reach the liver - or rarely other organs such as the lungs - and migrate to the skin in a secondary invasion movement. In the present case, the association with the placement of a Shilley catheter was already evident in the anamnesis, and the absence of evidence of amoebiasis in the complementary exams reinforces this pathogenesis. Subsequent hematogenous dissemination occurred, demonstrated by the presence of disseminated lesions, not only at the site of catheter implantation.
Diagnosis can be easily confirmed both by direct examination of lesion secretion (smear in ulcers, puncture of nodules/abscesses), and by histopathology which can demonstrate E. histolytica trophozoites on routine staining (Hematoxylin & eosin). Treatment is carried out with metronidazole in most cases, and other medications such as chloroquine, tinidazole, and emetine may be used, or surgical excision of lesions may be performed. Without a correct diagnosis and immediate treatment, it can result in serious morbidity and even death. The present patient was treated with metronidazole and ivermectin, and the catheter was also replaced, which did not show any parasites in laboratory tests. The patient showed a good therapeutic response and is being followed at the dermatology outpatient clinic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old female with chronic kidney disease presented to the dermatology department with painful, purulent-draining subcutaneous nodules and abscesses that began four months earlier at a right subclavian Shilley catheter site.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four months prior to presentation, nodular lesions and abscesses with purulent drainage developed at the implantation site of a right subclavian vein Shilley hemodialysis catheter and subsequently disseminated across the abdomen and anterior and posterior thorax. Empirical antibiotic courses of ciprofloxacin and cephalexin yielded no clinical improvement.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic kidney disease requiring temporary right subclavian Shilley catheter placement for hemodialysis during an acute episode 4 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful cutaneous nodules and draining abscesses over the chest and abdomen. Negative for fever, unintentional weight loss, or night sweats.

objective.physical_examination: Multiple painful subcutaneous nodules and tumors measuring up to 6 cm in largest diameter distributed across the abdomen and anterior/posterior thorax, covered by slightly desquamative erythematous-violaceous skin with central ulceration and spontaneous purulent drainage.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory tests before and after therapy showed normocytic, normochromic anemia secondary to chronic kidney disease and normal canalicular and transaminase liver enzymes. Three serial parasitological stool examinations were negative for helminths and protozoa.
objective.advanced_workup: Dermatological ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) of the largest posterior thoracic lesion showed negative aerobic, anaerobic, and mycobacterial cultures. Skin biopsy was performed for histopathology. CT scans of the abdomen and pelvis showed no hepatic or intestinal abscesses.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Direct parasitological microscopy of the ultrasound-guided FNAB aspirate identified cysts and trophozoites of Entamoeba histolytica, and skin biopsy histopathology (H&E stain) demonstrated a dermal histiocytic reaction surrounding superficial and deep dermal abscesses containing Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites, confirming primary/disseminated cutaneous amoebiasis associated with subclavian catheter placement. The patient was treated with oral metronidazole 250 mg every 8 hours for 20 days plus a single 12 mg dose of ivermectin and catheter replacement (catheter tip negative for parasites). At 30-day post-treatment follow-up, the nodules and tumors had regressed completely, leaving only residual hyperchromia.
